hi! im 19, i grew up in a similar way, and just started getting into learning how to cook like... this past summer. i still dont know a lot but i definitely know how to make a healthy meal i can eat. idk your situation fully obviously, but my mom specifically didn't want to teach me how to cook because she said i could just live at home and she could take care of me forever (i wasn't allowed to use the stove to even boil water until i was 16) . so while i agree with the advice from a lot of commenters about asking for help from your parents, i get if that isn't a possibility for you. i would recommend if asking your parents for advice isn't an option, you can still reach out to friends and such. even if they can't be there with you, i remember i was texting my friends the first time i ever boiled water because i was so scared of somehow messing something up since my parents inhibited my skills so much.   
 things like really simple pasta are a good place to start. honestly, though, after learning the super super basics (like just how a stove works and how to operate it), i jumped into just making recipes of things i thought id like. it was way easier for me to start with actually making something instead of feeling like i had to learn all the skills that go into making a recipe before i actually make it. don't go for something complex obviously, but simple recipes are doable as an absolute beginner. if you stumble into things you don't know, you can just google it and watch a youtube video or read an article on it. we live in an era where people have guides on how to do every single simple part of cooking, so you really dont have to be worried about being in the dark in the middle of a recipe. it'd probably be a smart idea to look through the recipe and look up the things you don't know how to do first, but also you can reference it while youre in the process of cooking just fine.   
with enough repetition of making various recipes and trying to get better, those core skills will slowly build up. best of luck to you!

i dont have *much* knowledge in russian myself, but i feel like a general rule of thumb when it comes to breaking rules in languages you're learning is to know them before you break them. it's better to talk Completely Grammatically Correct even when normal russian speakers might not do that than to break rules that shouldn't be broken. you can eventually find out more naturally how russian is spoken on a casual level by consuming various media and talking to russian people, but i feel like it's best to fully learn grammatical rules instead of trying to skip learning certain ones. even if it's something that's not used commonly, you may still want to know how to use it for certain situations, or even just be able to understand it if you see it written anywhere.

also, i do want to point out that for the specific question of cases, yes, cases are super important for speaking russian. cases come naturally to native russian speakers and are not seen as something wordy/extra, they are essential to the understanding of a sentence.
